title: Everyday English
description: Sharpen the English you use daily: polite requests, commonly confused words, agreement & tense, and clear writing.

stations.title: Greetings & Politeness
stations.summary: Register matters: the right level of formality makes requests land well.
points: 'Hello' is safe everywhere; 'Hi' is casual; 'Good morning' is more formal.
Introduce yourself with 'My name is Ani' or 'I'm Ani', and reply with 'Nice to meet you'.
'How are you?' is small talk — answer briefly: 'I'm good, thanks. And you?'
Soften requests: 'Could you ...' and 'Would it be possible to ...' sound far politer than bare imperatives.

questions.prompt: Which is the most polite way to ask a colleague for a favour?
options: Could you send me the file, please?
questions.explain: 'Could you ...' + 'please' turns an order into a request and keeps the relationship warm.

questions.prompt: Someone says 'Nice to meet you.' The natural reply is...
questions.explain: Add 'too' to return the same sentiment.

questions.prompt: 'How are you?' in everyday conversation is usually...
options: Small talk needing a short answer
A request for your life story
questions.explain: Answer briefly and bounce it back: 'Good, thanks. How about you?'

cards.back: Could you .../ Would it be possible to ...

stations.title: Commonly Confused Words
stations.summary: Small spelling choices change meaning — and readers notice.
points: their = belonging to them · there = a place · they're = they are.
your = belonging to you · you're = you are.
its = belonging to it · it's = it is (or it has).
affect = a verb (to influence) · effect = a noun (the result); 'a side effect', 'it affects me'.

questions.explain: 'They're' is short for 'they are'. Their shows possession; there points to a place.
'It's' means 'it is'. 'Its' is possessive: 'The train lost its last carriage.'
Affect is the verb (to influence); effect is the noun (a result): 'The effect was immediate.'

stations.title: Agreement & Tense
stations.summary: Most writing errors come from shaky agreement between subject and verb.
points: Present simple for habits and facts: 'I work from home.'
Present continuous for what is happening now: 'I am working right now.'
Third person singular takes -s: 'She goes to the office every day.'
Questions and negatives use do/does in the present simple: 'Do you like it?' 'She doesn't know.'

options: She is go to school daily.
questions.explain: Third person singular (she/he/it) takes -s in the present simple: goes.

questions.prompt: Which sentence describes something happening right now?
options: I am drinking coffee right now.
questions.explain: The present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) is used for actions in progress.
Use do/does for present simple questions: 'Do you like...', 'Does she like...'.

cards.back: Habits & facts: I work from home
She goes · He likes · It works

stations.title: Clear Writing & Directions
stations.summary: Good English at work is mostly short sentences and concrete requests.
points: Prefer short, concrete sentences: 'I'll send the summary by 3 pm.'
Give directions step by step: 'Go straight, then turn left at the lights.'
Ask for repetition politely: 'Could you repeat that, please?'
End emails with a clear next step so nobody has to guess.

questions.prompt: Which email opening suits a colleague you know well?
questions.explain: 'Hi <name>' is relaxed yet professional. 'Dear Sir/Madam' is for formal letters with no name.

options: I'll send the summary by 3 pm.
Regarding the summary, it may be possible that it will perhaps be sent at some point later.
It is what it is about the summary.
questions.explain: Short and concrete beats long and vague. State the action and the time.

options: Keep going straight, then turn left
questions.explain: Instructions are read in order: first go straight, then turn left.

cards.back: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?
